claims.text: Differences in strength and ductility among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets are governed by variations in stacking-fault energy and phase stability.
Stacking-fault energy and phase stability govern the generation and stabilization of twins and martensite.
Reducing the number of constituents tends to lower stacking-fault energy.
Reducing the number of constituents tends to alter phase equilibria in a way that enhances deformation-induced twinning or transformation-induced plasticity.
Deformation-induced defects can delay void nucleation.
Deformation-induced defects can delay void coalescence.
The candidate materials are to begin as thermomechanically processed, single-phase FCC alloys.
Constituent count and composition will be varied while processing conditions are held constant.
High-strain-rate and cryogenic deformation conditions promote planar-defect formation or phase transformation.
Reduced compositional complexity promotes a higher density of deformation twins.
Altered FCC phase stability can promote an FCC-to-BCC martensitic transformation.
BCC martensite formed from FCC can enhance strain hardening, strength, and ductility at cryogenic temperature.
Twins and martensitic phases impede dislocation motion.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will develop higher twin or martensite densities than equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni under identical loading.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will have higher work-hardening rates than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit later void coalescence than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit a superior strength-ductility balance relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
The proposed mechanism may not apply under quasi-static loading or when secondary-phase precipitation independently controls mechanical behavior.
Twin, stacking-fault, martensite, work-hardening, void-damage, strength, and ductility metrics will be measured in controlled comparative tests.
A lack of correlation between defect metrics and mechanical improvements, or a lack of statistically greater defect occurrence in the subsets, would refute the hypothesis.
